Concept 1 of 5 · the foundation

Classes & Objects

A class describes a kind of thing: what data each one carries and what it can do. Objects are the actual things. Each object has its own data, and they all share the behaviour written once in the class.

01

The idea

Imagine you are writing a game with fifty robots. Each robot has a name, a colour and a battery level, and each can greet you or recharge. Without classes you'd juggle fifty dictionaries and a pile of loose functions. With a class you write the description once, then stamp out as many robots as you need.

class
The blueprint. class Robot:
object / instance
One thing built from the class. zed = Robot("Zed", "teal")
attribute
Data stored on an object. zed.name
method
A function defined inside the class and called on an object. zed.greet()
__init__
Runs automatically right after a new object is created, to set up its attributes.
self
The object a method is working on. zed.greet() is shorthand for Robot.greet(zed).

Analogy

A cookie cutter and its cookies

The cutter (class) defines the shape. Every cookie (object) has that shape, but each one gets its own frosting (attribute values). Eating one cookie doesn't change the others, and you never eat the cutter.

Robot is the class, Robot("Zed", "teal") is a call that builds an object, and zed is just a name pointing at that object.

Concept 2 of 5 · pillar one

Inheritance

A class can be built on top of another class. The new class (the child or subclass) automatically gets everything the parent has, then adds new behaviour or replaces the parts that should work differently.

01

The idea

Inheritance models an "is-a" relationship. A dog is an animal, a manager is an employee, a square is a rectangle. Shared code lives once in the parent; each child only writes what makes it different.

  • Inherit: class Dog(Animal): gives Dog every attribute and method of Animal.
  • Extend: add new methods the parent doesn't have (fetch()).
  • Override: redefine a parent method with the same name (speak()). Python uses the child's version.
  • Reuse with super(): call the parent's version from inside the override, usually in __init__.

When you call rex.describe(), Python searches for describe on the object, then its class, then the parent, then the grandparent, all the way up to object. That search order is the MRO (method resolution order), and you can see it with Dog.__mro__.

Analogy

A family recipe book

Grandma's book has the base recipes. Your copy inherits all of them. You add a few of your own (extension) and cross out her cake recipe to write yours (override). For everything else, you just look it up in her pages.

Use inheritance for "is-a". For "has-a" (a car has an engine) store the other object as an attribute instead. That's called composition.

Concept 3 of 5 · pillar two

Polymorphism

"Many forms." The same operation works on objects of different types, and each object does the right thing for itself. The calling code doesn't need to know or check which type it's holding.

01

The idea

You already use polymorphism every day: len("hello"), len([1, 2]) and len({"a": 1}) are one function working on three types. Python gives you three ways to get the same power in your own classes:

  • Overriding: subclasses implement the same method differently (Circle.area() vs Square.area()).
  • Duck typing: no shared parent is needed at all. "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." Python only cares that the object has the method you call.
  • Operator overloading: special "dunder" methods teach built-ins your class. a + b calls a.__add__(b), len(x) calls x.__len__(), print(x) uses x.__str__().

The payoff: code like for s in shapes: total += s.area() never changes when you invent a new shape. You add a class; nothing else is touched.

Analogy

"Speak!" to a room full of animals

You give one command. The dog barks, the cat meows, the parrot says hello. You didn't need a separate instruction for each animal; each one knows how to respond to "speak".

Polymorphism leans on inheritance often, but not always. In Python, duck typing means any object with the right method fits.

Before and after: what happens when a new shape arrives?

02

Concept 4 of 5 · pillar three

Encapsulation

Bundle an object's data with the methods that work on it, and control how the outside world can touch that data. The goal is simple: the object should never end up in an invalid state.

01

The idea

A bank account must never have a negative deposit, and nobody should set its balance directly. Encapsulation puts those rules inside the class and gives the outside world a small, safe surface to work through.

Python doesn't have truly private variables. It relies on naming conventions and a little help from the language:

  • balance — public. Part of the interface; anyone may use it.
  • _balance — protected by convention. "Internal, please don't touch." Python doesn't stop you.
  • __balance — private via name mangling. Python renames it to _ClassName__balance, so acc.__balance fails. It prevents accidents and name clashes in subclasses, not determined access.
  • @property — makes a method look like an attribute, so you can add validation or make something read-only without changing how callers use it.

Analogy

A medicine capsule

The shell holds the ingredients together and decides how they get out. You don't scoop the powder out by hand; you take the capsule. A class is the shell, its attributes are the powder, and its methods are the only intended way in.

Python's motto here is "we're all consenting adults". Underscores communicate intent; they're a promise between programmers, not a lock.

Concept 5 of 5 · pillar four

Abstraction

Expose what an object does and hide how it does it. At the design level, abstraction also means defining a contract, a set of methods every implementation must provide, without saying how.

01

The idea

You drive a car through a steering wheel and two pedals. You don't manage fuel injection timing. The pedals are the abstraction: a simple interface over a complicated machine. In code, that shows up in two ways:

  • Everyday abstraction: any class whose public methods hide messy details. machine.make("latte") hides grinding, heating, brewing and frothing.
  • Abstract base classes (ABCs): from abc import ABC, abstractmethod lets you declare a contract. The ABC can't be instantiated, and every concrete subclass must implement each @abstractmethod or Python refuses to create it.

Abstraction pairs naturally with polymorphism: code written against the contract (PaymentMethod) works with every implementation (Card, PayPal, ones that don't exist yet).

Analogy

A wall socket

The socket is a contract: two holes, fixed voltage. A lamp, a laptop charger and a kettle all fit, and the power plant can switch from coal to solar without you changing your kettle. Neither side needs to know how the other works.

AbstractionEncapsulation
Main questionWhat should the outside world see?How is the inside protected?
LevelDesign: interfaces and contractsImplementation: data plus access rules
Python toolsABC, @abstractmethod, small public methods_name, __name, @property
ExamplePaymentMethod promises pay()__balance changes only through deposit()

Challenges

Final boss · all five concepts at once

Capstone: Mini Bank

Real programs use all five ideas together. Build the core of a tiny bank where every requirement exercises one concept. When every check passes, you've shown you can design with objects, not just recognise them.

AbstractionAccount is an abstract base class that promises monthly_interest().
EncapsulationThe balance lives in _balance behind a read-only property and guarded methods.
InheritanceSavingsAccount and CheckingAccount build on Account with super().
PolymorphismBank.apply_interest() treats every account the same way, with no type checks.
ClassesBank is a class too, with its own data, methods and __len__.
